strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: safety guidance for text diffusion models, an area that has received far less attention than autoregressive-model safety.

Provides a genuine technical contribution in Sec 3.3: deriving the discrete/masked-token analogue (Eq. 6) of the Gaussian kernel used in the original continuous-space safe denoiser, enabling tractable Monte Carlo approximation of the unsafe denoiser and β* for masked absorbing-state diffusion.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three distinct safety axes (hazard taxonomy compliance, jailbreak robustness, memorization/privacy) across multiple model families (MDLM, LLaDA-Base, LLaDA-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-Instruct) and multiple benchmarks (RTP, ToxiGen, BeaverTails, WildJailbreak, HarmBench, AdvBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, WikiText-103).

Extensive ablations on the three main hyperparameters (η, negation-set size N, active timestep window C) that give practitioners actionable guidance (e.g., early-window application, N≈500-1000 saturation).

Favorable efficiency comparison against training-free baselines (FK Steering, Best-of-N), showing comparable or better safety at substantially lower wall-clock cost, and showing SAD composes with an existing defense (DiffuGuard).

Good-faith attempt to explain anomalous results (cases where SAD appears to increase LlamaGuard unsafe rate) via a plausible style-shift/classifier-artifact hypothesis, cross-validated with refusal rate and HarmBench ASR trends.
Reproducibility materials are unusually thorough (full algorithm box, hyperparameter tables, prompt selection protocol, notation table, qualitative examples).
weaknesses: The central marketing claim of 'provably safe' guidance is weakened in the discrete setting: the exact β*(xt) requires intractable normalizing constants (Zsafe, Zunsafe), which are replaced by a freely tuned scalar η with no principled calibration to the true weight — so the practical algorithm is a heuristic approximation despite being motivated by Theorem 2.1, and this gap between the theory and what is actually implemented is not clearly acknowledged as a limitation.

The prompt-agnostic design (conditioning the unsafe denoiser on an empty prompt rather than the actual conditioning prompt) is an ad hoc simplification whose effect on the theoretical guarantee is not analyzed or justified beyond an informal modularity argument.

Effect sizes for hazard reduction are modest (e.g., ASR reduced from 38.4% to ~32-33% for MDLM, and from ~20% to ~15-18% for LLaDA) — safety is improved but far from resolved, which is not clearly stated as a limitation in the main text.

Jailbreak results are inconsistent: SAD sometimes worsens ASR under DIJA (e.g., LLaDA-1.5 DIJA in Table 2: 64.3→62.8 is a marginal gain, but Table 11 LLaDA-1.5 DIJA: 50.7→53.5, an increase; similar increases appear in several DIJA/self-reminder combinations across Tables 12-18), and the paper does not fully reconcile why the method fails specifically against DIJA while working well against PAD.

The negation-set-matching effect (RTP negation set works best on RTP-conditioned prompts) suggests SAD's effectiveness may be narrowly tied to distributional overlap with the reference set, raising doubts about generalization to novel or adversarially distributed unsafe content not covered by the curated negation set.

Utility preservation is not uniformly clean: e.g., BERTScore drops noticeably for the ToxiGen negation set on MDLM (−0.023) and for larger η/negation-set values, undermining the claim that SAD reliably preserves quality across settings; no human evaluation of fluency/quality is reported, relying solely on BERTScore/perplexity/PPL proxies.

The classifier-artifact explanation for unsafe-rate increases under SAD is plausible but relies on citing a separate paper's general finding rather than direct human verification of the specific outputs in this paper's experiments.

The method requires per-model, per-attack tuning of η and the active window C, which somewhat undercuts the claimed 'lightweight, plug-and-play' nature of the approach, since optimal configurations vary substantially across models and datasets.

Memorization evaluation is conducted on a single, relatively small fine-tuned MDLM model on WikiText-103, limiting generalizability of memorization-reduction claims to larger, more realistic pretraining-scale settings.

No comparison against a retraining/fine-tuning safety baseline (e.g., safety-tuned checkpoint) is provided to contextualize how much of the achievable safety gain SAD captures relative to an upper-bound alternative.

strengths: Principled theoretical grounding: the paper extends the training-free 'safe denoiser' identity (Kim et al., 2025) from continuous image diffusion to discrete masked text diffusion, deriving the categorical forward-kernel factorization needed for the safe/unsafe denoiser estimators (Sec. 3.3, eq. 7). This is a non-trivial and largely correct adaptation.

Comprehensive empirical scope: the method is evaluated across three distinct safety axes (hazard taxonomy, jailbreak robustness, memorization) on multiple backbones (MDLM, LLaDA-Base/Instruct/1.5, Dream-Instruct) and multiple benchmarks (RTP, ToxiGen, BeaverTails, WildJailbreak, HarmBench, AdvBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, WikiText-103).

Extensive ablations on the three main hyperparameters (N, η, time window C) and a throughput analysis, giving practitioners useful guidance (e.g., N≈500-1000 saturates gains, early/short windows preserve utility).

Demonstrated modularity/compositionality with an existing diffusion-specific defense (DiffuGuard) and comparison against training-free alternatives (FK Steering, Best-of-N), showing comparable safety at much lower computational cost.

Unusually candid limitations discussion (Sec. 6, Appendix F): the authors explicitly note that the practical estimator departs from the exact identity (relaxed kernel, length normalization, logit-space combination, one-sided β), that no approximation bound exists, and that automatic judges may be biased by output style — this transparency is a genuine strength.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility documentation (hyperparameter tables, dataset/negation-set construction, evaluation metric definitions) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The abstract/intro claims text is steered toward 'provably safe regions,' but the deployed estimator (Appendix A) is heavily heuristic: a relaxed kernel with an arbitrary clipped γ, length-normalized log-scores that are 'no longer unbiased,' a hand-tuned scalar η replacing the intractable normalizing constants, and an ad hoc logit-space combination rule instead of the additive correction implied by Thm. 2.1. The theoretical guarantee is essentially lost in practice, so the 'provable' framing overstates what is actually delivered.

Results are inconsistent and sometimes go the wrong direction: in several jailbreak tables (e.g., Tables 11, 13, 15, 17) the Llama-Guard unsafe rate frequently *increases* under SAD, and DIJA ASR sometimes increases too (e.g., LLaDA-1.5 HarmBench DIJA: 50.7→53.5). These are explained post-hoc as 'classifier artifacts from style shift' without independent verification (no human annotation study), which is a somewhat unfalsifiable excuse for unfavorable results.

No human evaluation anywhere despite the paper itself acknowledging that automatic safety/refusal judges can be fooled by stylistic shifts in both directions (a false-negative example is even shown in Appendix D.2, Example 2, where a partially-mitigated harmful campaign is scored 'safe'). This substantially undermines confidence in the headline ASR/unsafe-rate numbers.

Heavy, per-setting hyperparameter tuning (η, N, and especially the critical timestep window C, which the ablations show has the largest qualitative effect) is required to obtain good safety-utility tradeoffs, undercutting the claimed 'lightweight' and easily-deployable nature of the method; no principled rule for selecting C is given beyond 'early is better,' determined empirically per model/attack.

The core partition assumption (Dsafe ≫ Dunsafe, known/exactly separable) is stated as matching pretraining practice, but the effectiveness of the negation set is shown to be highly sensitive to how well it matches the test distribution (RTP-conditioned prompts respond best to an RTP negation set), suggesting the method is less 'universal' than advertised and requires domain-matched curation per threat.

Training-free baseline comparisons (FK Steering, Best-of-N) are only conducted on MDLM/RTP and not extended to the jailbreak or LLaDA settings, leaving the comparative efficiency/quality claims less broadly supported.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to Kim et al. (2025): the main new contribution is the discrete categorical kernel derivation (Sec. 3.3), which, while useful, is a relatively straightforward re-derivation of an established framework for a new data modality, and two concurrent works (Lee & Han 2026; An & Han 2026) address closely related steering ideas for the same models.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: safety mechanisms for text diffusion models, which differ structurally from AR-LLMs and for which existing safety tooling does not directly transfer.

The paper is grounded in a principled theoretical identity (the safe-denoiser decomposition of Kim et al., 2025) and does the nontrivial work of deriving the discrete/masked-diffusion analogue (categorical kernel factorization, Sec. 3.3), which is a genuine technical contribution beyond simply copy-pasting the continuous-domain method.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three distinct safety dimensions (hazard taxonomy, memorization, jailbreak robustness) across multiple models (MDLM, LLaDA, LLaDA-1.5, Dream) and multiple benchmarks, with substantial ablations on η, negation-set size, and timestep windows.

Unusually candid limitations and appendix discussion: the authors openly acknowledge that βˆ ignores the safe-side of the odds, that no approximation bound exists between practical SAD and the exact identity, that automatic judges can be fooled by style shifts, and provide a qualitative example where their own method's output is (in their view) mis-scored as safe by the judge -- this transparency is commendable.

Reasonable efficiency profile is demonstrated relative to particle-based alternatives (FK Steering) and post-hoc filtering (Best-of-N), and the paper attempts to test compositionality with an existing defense (DiffuGuard).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core theoretical contribution is an application/adaptation of an existing image-diffusion safe-denoiser framework (Kim et al., 2025) to a new domain, and the central algorithmic novelty (the categorical kernel factorization) is a relatively short, mechanical derivation once the masking process is written down.

The gap between the 'provably safe' framing used in the abstract/introduction and what is actually implemented is large and, to this reviewer, understates a real problem: the practical estimator replaces the strict forward kernel with an ad hoc relaxed kernel, renormalizes by length, discards the safe-side denominator of β*, treats η as a free uncalibrated hyperparameter, and applies the correction in log-space rather than the form given by the theorem. The paper itself (Appendix A, Sec. 6) admits this reduces the method to 'not a safety certificate,' yet the framing throughout the main text ('provably safe regions,' 'derived from an exact identity') oversells the guarantees actually delivered.

No formal approximation/error bound is provided between the practical estimator and the exact safe denoiser identity, and the authors acknowledge this (Appendix F); given the observed non-monotonicity in η and sensitivity to time-window, this absence is a meaningful gap for a paper whose main selling point is theoretical grounding.

Effect sizes are modest and highly attack-dependent: DIJA-based jailbreaks are only marginally affected (often <2pp change, occasionally slightly worse), while gains are concentrated on PAD; several configurations actually increase Llama-Guard unsafe rate (e.g., Table 9, Table 11, Table 13, Table 15 zero-shot rows), which the authors attribute post hoc to judge/style artifacts without independent human verification to confirm this explanation.

Reported headline numbers (Tables 2, 9-17) are explicitly the 'best-performing configuration' per defense/attack rather than a single fixed hyperparameter setting evaluated uniformly; combined with the demonstrated high sensitivity of results to η and the timestep window C, this raises concerns about cherry-picking and about how well the reported gains would hold under a realistic, non-oracle hyperparameter selection procedure.

Heavy reliance on automatic safety/refusal judges (Llama-Guard-3-8B, HarmBench classifier) whose potential unreliability under style shift is explicitly acknowledged by the authors as a confound for both false positives and false negatives (Appendix D.2 example), yet no human evaluation is conducted anywhere in the paper to validate or correct these metrics -- a substantial reproducibility/validity gap for a paper making safety claims.

The method requires per-model, per-dataset hyperparameter tuning of η, N, and the timestep window C, undercutting the claimed 'lightweight, plug-and-play' advantage over training-based approaches; the extensive appendix sweeps needed to find workable settings suggest the method is not straightforwardly deployable without similar tuning effort in new settings.

Memorization experiments are conducted on a single small-scale fine-tuned MDLM model on WikiText-103 only, limiting generality of the memorization claims relative to the hazard/jailbreak experiments conducted on larger models.

Comparisons to the two closest concurrent works (Lee & Han 2026; An & Han 2026) are discussed only qualitatively in related work, with no direct empirical head-to-head comparison, making it hard to assess SAD's relative merit against the most similar existing inference-time steering methods.

strengths: Non-trivial technical adaptation: the paper derives a discrete/categorical analogue (Sec 3.3, Appendix A) of the continuous 'safe denoiser' identity for masked absorbing-state text diffusion, which is a genuine (if incremental relative to Kim et al. 2025) contribution rather than a naive application.

Unusually comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three distinct safety dimensions (hazard taxonomy, memorization, jailbreak robustness), four models (MDLM, LLaDA-Base/Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-Instruct), multiple negation-set sources, and five jailbreak benchmarks with three attack types, which gives reasonable confidence that observed trends are not artifacts of a single setup.

Demonstrates modularity/compositionality with existing defenses (PPL filtering, self-reminder, DiffuGuard) and favorable efficiency versus a particle-based training-free baseline (FK Steering), supporting the practical/deployment relevance claim.

Unusually candid and detailed limitations discussion (Sec 6, Appendix F): explicitly flags that the deployed estimator departs from the exact theoretical identity in three ways, that beta-hat ignores the safe-side of the odds, that no approximation bound exists, and includes a qualitative example where the paper's own judge mislabels a partially-mitigated jailbreak output as safe -- this level of self-scrutiny strengthens trust in the reported results.

Thorough hyperparameter ablations (eta, negation-set size N, timestep window C) with sensible, interpretable trends (e.g., saturation around N=500-1000, importance of early-window guidance) that aid reproducibility and practical deployment guidance.
weaknesses: The abstract/intro frame the method as steering toward 'provably safe' regions, but the actually deployed estimator (relaxed kernel, length-normalized biased beta-hat, logit-space correction) is explicitly acknowledged to forfeit the exactness/unbiasedness of the underlying identity; the 'provable' framing is therefore somewhat overstated relative to what is empirically run.

Effect sizes are frequently modest and inconsistent: hazard-taxonomy ASR reductions are ~5-6 points (Table 1), and jailbreak results under DIJA are frequently negligible or even reversed (e.g., LLaDA-1.5 DIJA under 'None': 64.3->62.8; under DiffuGuard: 53.5->53.5), undercutting the claim of consistently 'substantial' unsafe-generation reduction.

All safety/refusal metrics rely on automatic judges (Llama-Guard-3-8B, HarmBench classifier), and the paper itself documents cases where SAD increases the Llama-Guard unsafe rate (attributed to style-shift artifacts) and a case where a partially-mitigated harmful output is judged safe; without any human evaluation, it is not possible to fully rule out that some reported gains/losses are judge artifacts rather than real safety changes.

The core safety-guidance hyperparameter eta requires per-model and per-negation-set retuning (values differ substantially across MDLM, LLaDA-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5) and is not accompanied by a principled selection criterion, which weakens the 'lightweight, flexible, plug-and-play' claims made for the method.

The negation-set-only (one-sided) formulation is acknowledged to discard the safe-side term of the exact posterior odds, meaning beta-hat cannot distinguish 'close to unsafe set' from 'close to everything,' which the authors identify as a core reason for the observed non-monotonic and sometimes fragile eta behavior.
For LLaDA, the training corpus is undisclosed, so the claimed 'in-distribution' comparison and the interpretation of results for one of the two primary models rests on an unverifiable assumption.
